report:
## What the Evidence Shows

Your sister's belief — that a higher *number* of vaccines given in childhood increases autism risk — has been directly and repeatedly tested, and the scientific consensus does not support it.

**Origins of the claim:** Autism-vaccine fears trace largely to a 1998 paper by Andrew Wakefield in *The Lancet* linking the MMR vaccine to autism in 12 children. That study was later found to involve data manipulation and undisclosed financial conflicts of interest; it was retracted in 2010, and Wakefield lost his medical license ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancet_MMR_vaccine-autism_report)).

**Direct test of the "too many vaccines" hypothesis:** A key CDC-funded study by DeStefano et al. (2013) specifically examined whether the *cumulative number of antigens* (immune-stimulating substances) children received from vaccines in their first two years was associated with autism. It found no relationship between increasing antigen exposure and autism risk ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23545349/)).

**Broader body of evidence:** A comprehensive review in *Vaccine* concluded that despite extensive scrutiny — including studies on MMR, thimerosal, and vaccine timing/number — the overwhelming majority of high-quality evidence refutes a causal vaccine-autism link ([ScienceDirect/PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8694782/)). A large 2025 Danish study of over 1 million children also found no link between aluminum adjuvants (used in multiple vaccines) and autism or other chronic conditions ([Healthline](https://www.healthline.com/health-news/research-finds-no-evidence-vaccines-cause-autism)).

**Recent controversy:** In late 2025, the CDC website was controversially edited under new HHS leadership to suggest the link hasn't been ruled out — but independent fact-checkers and pediatric experts noted this contradicts the actual body of research ([FactCheck.org](https://www.factcheck.org/2025/11/revised-cdc-website-about-autism-and-vaccines-is-not-evidence-based/)).

**Bottom line:** The specific claim that more vaccines (or more antigens) causes more autism has been tested directly and not supported by rigorous, large-scale studies.
